summary: AstroVitals is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on deep-space missions, where Earth is too far away for real-time medical support. It builds a personal baseline for each crew member, scores risk continuously on board, and gives plain-language alerts with first-response guidance. Alerts are queued for Earth with a realistic communication delay.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
It streams four vitals for each astronaut (heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, temperature) and a cabin CO₂ reading. It compares each vital with that person’s own baseline using z-scores. These are combined into a 0–100 risk score with three states: Nominal, Watch and Alert. Planned exertion such as an EVA is recognised so it doesn’t trigger false alarms. When status worsens, the crew gets an instant alert with guidance (for example, an infection triage checklist for fever). The same alert is queued for the ground team and arrives after the selected delay (none, 4 or 22 minutes). The demo lets you inject a CO₂ scrubber fault, a fever, sleep loss or an EVA and watch the response.

What benefits does it have?

  • The crew gets help immediately instead of waiting for Earth.
  • Each person is judged against their own normal, so small drifts are caught early.
  • Fewer false alarms, because planned activity is recognised.
  • It runs fully on board, so it works when the link is delayed or down.
  • It shows the whole crew in one view, which helps a small crew with limited medical training.

What is the intended impact?
Safer long-duration missions by catching problems early, with the crew acting on its own during communication gaps. The same approach could later help remote clinics, polar stations and other isolated settings on Earth.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with SVG for the heart-rate trend lines. No external libraries.
  • Software: Claude (Anthropic) to write the code and slides; the demo and deck are hosted as Claude artifacts.
  • Hardware: none. Data is simulated. A real version would take input from wearable sensors and a cabin air monitor.
